Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in Michigan: monthly grocery benefit for seniors on fixed incomes

contentSections.title: Renters Qualify Too
contentSections.body: This credit is widely associated with homeowners, but Michigan renters are also eligible. The state treats a portion of your parent's rent as equivalent to a property tax payment. Renters age 65 or older have access to a separate alternate calculation (Worksheet 5) that can return up to $1,900. If your parent has been renting for years and has never claimed this credit, there may be multiple years of missed refunds worth recovering.

contentSections.title: The Four-Year Retroactive Window
contentSections.body: Michigan Treasury allows seniors to file amended returns and claim this credit for up to four prior tax years. If your parent has not been aware of this program, or has been filing without claiming the credit, those missed years may still be recoverable. Each year requires its own MI-1040CR completed with the income figures and property tax or rent amounts for that specific year. Use the instructions booklet from each respective year.

contentSections.title: How Total Household Resources (THR) Differs from Your Tax Return Income
contentSections.body: THR is the income measure Michigan uses to determine eligibility and calculate the credit. It is broader than federal adjusted gross income (AGI). THR includes Social Security benefits (even the nontaxable portion), pension and retirement distributions, interest and dividends, and other income that may not appear in federal AGI. Because THR can be higher than the number on your parent's federal return, it is important to calculate it carefully using the MI-1040CR instructions. Families who use federal AGI by mistake often undercount income, which can affect both eligibility and the size of the credit.

faqs.question: My parent rents and has never filed Michigan state taxes. Can they still get this credit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Renters qualify for this credit, and filing Michigan state taxes is the mechanism for claiming it. Even if your parent had no other reason to file Michigan taxes, they can file Form MI-1040 with MI-1040CR to claim the credit. If they are age 65 or older, they should also complete Worksheet 5 to check whether the alternate renter method produces a larger refund. They can go back up to four prior years.

faqs.question: My parent's income comes mostly from Social Security and a small pension. Does that count against them?
faqs.answer: Yes, both count toward Total Household Resources (THR). Social Security benefits, including the nontaxable portion, are included in THR. So are pension distributions. THR must stay below $71,500 for any credit to apply. The credit phases down by 10% for each $1,000 of THR above $62,500. A parent with THR around $65,000, for example, would see the credit reduced but not eliminated.

faqs.question: Can I apply on my parent's behalf if they are unable to manage their own taxes?
faqs.answer: Yes. If you have power of attorney or are your parent's legal representative, you can prepare and file the return on their behalf. Indicate the representative's relationship on the return per Michigan Treasury's instructions. AARP Tax-Aide, reachable at (888) 227-7669, offers free tax preparation assistance and can work with caregivers who bring documentation for a parent who cannot attend in person.

faqs.question: My parent owns their home. Is there a limit on how much the property can be worth?
faqs.answer: Yes, for homeowners. The taxable value of the homestead must fall under the annual cap stated in the MI-1040CR instructions. That cap is updated each year by Michigan Treasury. Check the instructions for the specific year being filed. Note that taxable value is not the same as market value or assessed value; it is typically lower. Renters do not face a property-value cap.

faqs.question: My parent missed claiming this credit for the past three years. Is that money gone?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Michigan Treasury allows retroactive claims for up to four years from the year the credit could have been claimed. To recover prior years, file an amended Michigan return for each year using the MI-1040CR from that specific tax year, with the income and housing figures from that year. The Michigan Treasury individual income tax line at (517) 636-4486 can confirm the process for your parent's situation.

faqs.question: My parent lives in a mobile home and pays both rent and property taxes. Which rules apply?
faqs.answer: Mobile home situations can involve either renter or homeowner rules depending on whether your parent owns the mobile home or rents it, and whether they pay property taxes separately or through lot rent. The MI-1040CR instructions address mobile home situations specifically. Because the calculation can go either way, review the instructions carefully or use a free tax preparer through AARP Tax-Aide at (888) 227-7669.

faqs.question: Can my parent claim this credit and the Michigan Home Heating Credit in the same year?
faqs.answer: Yes. These are separate credits filed on separate forms. The Homestead Property Tax Credit uses MI-1040CR. The Home Heating Credit uses MI-1040CR-7 and has its own income limits and calculation. Many Michigan seniors qualify for both. A tax preparer at an AARP Tax-Aide site can calculate both credits at the same time at no cost.

faqs.question: What if my parent's total household resources are just over the $71,500 limit?
faqs.answer: No credit is available once THR reaches or exceeds $71,500. However, if THR is between $62,500 and $71,500, a partial credit still applies; it phases down by 10% for each $1,000 above $62,500. It is worth calculating even if THR is close to the limit. If your parent's income is near the edge, double-check that THR is being calculated correctly using the MI-1040CR instructions, since errors in the income calculation are common.

programs.name: Home-Delivered Meals
programs.tagline: If your parent is 60+ and homebound in Michigan, they may qualify for free nutritious meals delivered to their door, no income test required.

localEntities.name: Local Meals on Wheels or senior nutrition providers

programs.intro:
Michigan's Home-Delivered Meals program delivers nutritious meals directly to older adults who are homebound or unable to shop and cook on their own. Unlike most government benefits, this program has no income limit and no asset test. Eligibility is based on age (60+), homebound status, and nutritional need, not on how much money your parent has.

The number of meals your parent receives is determined by a local assessment of their individual situation. Delivery schedules, meal formats (hot versus frozen), and exact intake processes vary by region. Some areas deliver Monday through Friday; others include frozen meals for weekends and holidays. The state says there is no cost to participate, though most local programs invite a voluntary contribution toward the meal.

This program is run through local Area Agencies on Aging and their partner providers, including Meals on Wheels affiliates. There is no central state application number. Your first step is finding and contacting the Area Agency on Aging that serves your parent's county.
programs.savingsSource: Free service; the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services states there is no cost for meals, though local programs may suggest a voluntary donation contribution.

summary: Age 60 or older
Homebound or unable to shop and prepare meals
At high nutritional risk (due to illness, hospitalization, living alone, or inability to cook)
No income limit
No asset test
structuredEligibility.functionalRequirement: Your parent must be homebound or otherwise unable to obtain food or prepare meals under normal circumstances. This is assessed locally and typically means your parent has difficulty leaving the home due to illness, disability, recent hospitalization, or a lack of ability to shop or cook safely.
otherRequirements: Must be at high nutritional risk due to factors such as illness, recent hospitalization, living alone, or inability to shop or cook.
Family members with disabilities who permanently live in the home of the eligible older adult may also be eligible.
Local providers may have their own screening criteria or priority rules that affect wait times or eligibility determination.

applicationGuide.summary: Call your local Area Agency on Aging; they can screen your parent, complete an intake interview, and start service within a few days depending on local capacity.

steps.title: Find your local Area Agency on Aging
steps.description: Michigan is divided into regional service areas, each served by a different Area Agency on Aging. Use the Michigan MDHHS program page at michigan.gov/mdhhs/assistance-programs/other-help/food/home-delivered-meals to find the agency covering your parent's county, or call the Eldercare Locator at (800) 677-1116 to get a referral to the right local office.

steps.title: Call your local Area Agency on Aging
steps.description: Contact the agency directly by phone. Tell them your parent is 60+, homebound, and has difficulty shopping or preparing meals. They will screen for eligibility and schedule an intake assessment.

steps.title: Complete the intake interview or assessment
steps.description: A local coordinator will ask about your parent's homebound status, any recent hospitalization or medical concerns, and their nutritional needs. Have your parent's address, phone number, and a brief description of why they cannot shop or cook ready for this call.

steps.title: Confirm delivery schedule and details
steps.description: Once approved, the local provider will explain the meal schedule, whether meals are hot or frozen, delivery days, and whether someone needs to be home at the time of delivery. Ask specifically about weekend meals if your parent needs them, since coverage varies by region.

applicationGuide.processingTime: Service can begin within a few days of application, depending on local capacity and assessment. Timelines vary by Area Agency on Aging.
applicationGuide.waitlist: No statewide waitlist exists, but local waiting lists may exist depending on the Area Agency on Aging or meal provider in your parent's county. Ask the local agency directly about current availability.
applicationGuide.tip: When you call, mention any recent hospital discharge or medical diagnosis. This can strengthen your parent's nutritional risk classification and may affect how quickly service starts.

A brief description of why your parent is homebound or unable to shop and cook (illness, disability, recent hospital discharge, or similar)
Information about any recent hospitalization or medical or nutritional concerns that affect your parent's ability to obtain food

contacts.description: Visit the official state program page for program details and links to regional providers. This page does not handle applications directly.

contacts.description: Number listed on michigan.gov

contentSections.title: This is not an income-based program
contentSections.body: Many families assume their parent earns too much to qualify, or that owning a home or having savings disqualifies them. This program does not have an income limit or an asset test. If your parent is 60+, homebound, and struggling to shop or prepare meals, they may qualify regardless of their financial situation.

contentSections.title: What varies by region
contentSections.body: Because this program is administered locally, details differ significantly depending on where your parent lives. Some areas deliver hot meals Monday through Friday. Others deliver frozen meals for weekends and holidays. Delivery days, meal types, and suggested donation amounts all depend on the local provider. When you call your Area Agency on Aging, ask specifically about delivery frequency, whether meals are hot or frozen, and whether your parent needs to be home to accept the delivery.

faqs.question: My parent owns their home and has savings. Does that disqualify them?
faqs.answer: No. Michigan's Home-Delivered Meals program has no income limit and no asset test. Eligibility is based on age (60+), homebound status, and nutritional need. Your parent's savings, home value, or retirement income does not affect whether they qualify.

faqs.question: How many meals will my parent actually receive?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed statewide number of meals. The local Area Agency on Aging or their meal provider conducts an individual assessment and determines how many meals your parent needs based on that evaluation. The number can range from a few meals per week to daily delivery. Ask the local agency directly after the intake assessment.

faqs.question: Is there a waitlist, and how long is it?
faqs.answer: There is no statewide waitlist, but individual local providers may have one depending on their capacity. Some areas can start service within a few days; others may have a wait. When you call your local Area Agency on Aging, ask directly about current availability in your parent's zip code.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my parent, or do they have to call themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes, a family caregiver can call on behalf of an older parent. Be prepared to describe your parent's situation: why they are homebound, whether they have had a recent hospitalization, and why they cannot shop or prepare meals independently. The intake coordinator may want to speak with your parent at some point in the process, but initiating the call on their behalf is fine.

faqs.question: My parent lives with a family member who has a disability. Can that person also receive meals?
faqs.answer: Possibly. Michigan's program states that family members with disabilities who permanently live in the home of the eligible older adult may also be eligible for meals. Confirm this with your local Area Agency on Aging when you call, since local providers may apply their own rules.

faqs.question: Can my parent receive Home-Delivered Meals and SNAP at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes. These are separate programs with separate eligibility rules. Home-Delivered Meals is funded through the Older Americans Act and has no income test. SNAP is income-based. If your parent qualifies for both, receiving one does not affect the other. You can apply for SNAP through the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services at michigan.gov or by calling (855) 275-6424.

programs.tagline: If your parent already receives SSI in Michigan, they may be getting a small state cash supplement automatically; knowing the current amounts helps you catch if a payment is wrong.

programs.intro:
If your parent receives federal Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and lives in Michigan, they are also receiving a small state cash supplement added on top of their federal SSI payment. This is not a separate application; the supplement is attached automatically once SSI eligibility is established. What changes is the amount: where your parent lives determines how much the state adds.

For 2026, the state supplement ranges from $7 per month (for someone in a Medicaid-funded facility) up to $179.30 per month (for someone in a home for the aged). People living independently or in someone else's household receive $9.33 to $14 per month, paid quarterly rather than monthly. People in licensed care settings such as domiciliary care, personal care facilities, or homes for the aged receive higher monthly amounts. The full combined payment (federal SSI plus Michigan supplement) for a single person living independently is $1,008 per month in 2026.

The program splits administration between two agencies. Social Security administers the supplement for most living arrangements. Michigan's Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) administers it for others, particularly licensed care settings. Because of that split, families sometimes get confused about where to call when something seems wrong. This page explains what your parent should be receiving, who pays it, and what to do if the amount looks off.

applicationGuide.summary: There is no separate Michigan supplement application; apply for federal SSI through Social Security and the supplement is calculated automatically once eligibility and living arrangement are confirmed.

steps.title: Apply for federal SSI
steps.description: Call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY: 1-800-325-0778), apply online at ssa.gov/ssi, or visit your local Social Security office. You cannot get the Michigan supplement without first being approved for federal SSI. If your parent is already receiving SSI, skip to Step 3.

steps.title: Report your parent's living arrangement accurately
steps.description: The Michigan supplement amount depends entirely on where your parent lives: independently, in your home, in a domiciliary care facility, a personal care facility, a home for the aged, or a Medicaid-funded facility. Social Security and MDHHS use this information to assign the correct supplement category. If living arrangement changes later, report it promptly because an incorrect category means an incorrect payment.

steps.title: Confirm which agency administers the supplement
steps.description: For most living arrangements (independent, household of another, with an essential person), SSA administers the supplement and it flows through the same SSI payment process. For licensed care settings (domiciliary care, personal care facility, home for the aged), MDHHS may administer it. If you are unsure which agency handles your parent's category, call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 and ask directly.

steps.title: Verify the payment amount and schedule
steps.description: People in the independent and household-of-another categories receive the supplement quarterly, not monthly: payments arrive in March, June, September, and December by paper check or direct deposit. People in licensed care settings receive the supplement monthly. Cross-check the published 2026 rates at ssa.gov against what your parent receives to catch any discrepancy.

steps.title: Report any change in living arrangement
steps.description: If your parent moves from living independently to a personal care facility, or from a home for the aged to a Medicaid nursing facility, the supplement category changes and so does the amount. Call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 within 10 days of any move to report the change and avoid an overpayment that SSA would later collect back.

applicationGuide.processingTime: The Michigan supplement is calculated as part of the SSI award process. No separate Michigan processing time is published. SSI applications typically take 3 to 6 months; once SSI is approved and living arrangement is confirmed, the supplement is included in the next payment cycle.
applicationGuide.tip: If your parent is already on SSI and you are not sure whether they are receiving the Michigan supplement, ask SSA for a benefit breakdown when you call. The supplement should appear as a line item separate from the federal SSI amount.

applicationNotes: The Michigan supplement is not paid as a separate check in most cases; for people living independently or in another person's household, the supplement arrives quarterly (March, June, September, December), not with the monthly SSI payment. If your parent expects a monthly supplement and it is not arriving, call SSA to confirm the payment schedule for their specific living arrangement.

If your parent moves to a licensed care setting, the supplement category changes and MDHHS may take over administration from SSA. Notify SSA within 10 days of any move. Failure to report a change can result in an overpayment that SSA will collect back, sometimes by reducing future SSI payments.

Income reduces the combined SSI payment starting with the federal portion first. Only after the federal SSI payment is reduced to zero does countable income begin to reduce the Michigan supplement. This means the supplement may be partially or fully paid even when the federal SSI payment has been reduced by income.
Published supplement amounts change over time as SSA updates its tables. Verify the current year's rates directly at ssa.gov before relying on any figure you find elsewhere, including this page.

contentSections.title: Two agencies administer this supplement
contentSections.body: SSA handles the supplement for people living independently, in another person's household, or with an essential person. MDHHS handles it for people in domiciliary care, personal care facilities, homes for the aged, and Medicaid facilities. If you call SSA about a care-facility supplement issue and they say it is not their program, follow up with MDHHS at 1-800-642-3195.

faqs.question: My parent is already on SSI. Do they need to do anything to get the Michigan supplement?
faqs.answer: No separate application is needed. The supplement is calculated automatically as part of the SSI payment process once SSI eligibility and living arrangement are confirmed. If your parent is on SSI and you are not sure whether they are receiving the supplement, call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 and ask for a breakdown of their current benefit, including the state supplement line item.

faqs.question: My parent moved from living with us into an assisted living facility. Does the supplement amount change?
faqs.answer: Yes, and significantly. A person living in a household of another receives only $9.33 per month in state supplement. The same person in a personal care facility receives $157.50 per month, and in a home for the aged, $179.30 per month. Report the move to SSA at 1-800-772-1213 within 10 days. The new rate takes effect once SSA updates the living arrangement category. Missing this update can cause either underpayment or overpayment, both of which create problems to correct later.

faqs.question: Why does my parent in a nursing home only get $7 per month in state supplement when others get much more?
faqs.answer: Federal and state policy sets a very low SSI and supplement amount for people in Medicaid-funded facilities because Medicaid is already paying for room, board, and care. The $7 monthly supplement is intended as a small personal-needs allowance on top of the $44 federal SSI personal needs amount, for a combined $44 total monthly payment (the federal and state amounts together equal the published $44 combined rate for Medicaid facility residents in 2026). This is the published rate; it is not an error.

faqs.question: My parent's house is worth far more than $2,000. Does that disqualify them from SSI and the supplement?
faqs.answer: No. The primary home your parent lives in is fully excluded from the SSI resource calculation regardless of its value. The $2,000 resource limit applies to countable assets such as cash, bank balances, and stocks. Owning a home does not count against that limit as long as your parent lives there.

faqs.question: Can I apply for SSI on behalf of my elderly parent if they cannot do it themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. You can contact SSA on your parent's behalf and be designated as their representative payee, which allows you to manage their benefit. Call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 to start the SSI application and ask about the representative payee process. If your parent has a legal guardian or power of attorney, bring that documentation to the appointment or have it available when you call.

faqs.question: My parent receives SSI in another state and is moving to Michigan. Do they need to reapply?
faqs.answer: SSI itself transfers with the person; they do not lose SSI eligibility by moving to Michigan. However, the Michigan state supplement is not the same amount as what other states pay, and your parent must notify SSA of the move and new address. The Michigan supplement will then be calculated based on their Michigan living arrangement. Call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 before or immediately after the move to report the address change.

faqs.question: The supplement for people living independently is paid quarterly, not monthly. How do I make sure my parent does not miss a payment?
faqs.answer: Quarterly payments arrive in March, June, September, and December. If your parent has direct deposit set up, verify those months that the deposit appears. If they receive a paper check, confirm the mailing address on file with SSA is current. A missed quarterly payment should be reported to SSA at 1-800-772-1213 promptly, not at the end of the year.

faqs.question: Can my parent receive both the Michigan SSI supplement and SNAP at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes. SSI recipients in Michigan are generally categorically eligible for SNAP (food assistance), meaning SSI approval can streamline or establish SNAP eligibility without a separate income or resource determination. Apply for SNAP through the Michigan MDHHS website at michigan.gov/mdhhs or by calling 1-888-642-7434. Being on SSI does not reduce or eliminate SNAP benefits.

programs.name: Home Help Program
programs.tagline: If your parent has Medicaid and needs hands-on help with bathing, dressing, or other daily tasks, Michigan may pay for a trained aide to come to their home.

localEntities.name: Local county MDHHS office where the client resides
Michigan Department of Health and Human Services provider/program page for Home Help

programs.intro:
Michigan's Home Help Program pays for personal care aides to come to your parent's home and assist with daily tasks they can no longer do safely on their own. That can include bathing, dressing, grooming, getting in and out of bed, preparing meals, doing laundry, and taking medications. If your parent is on Medicaid and struggling with even one of these tasks, this program may cover real, scheduled help at no cost to them.

This is not a cash payment to your family. It is an authorization for services, meaning the state pays an aide directly after your parent's needs are assessed. The number of hours approved is based on what the MDHHS Adult Services Worker determines your parent needs; there is no fixed statewide cap or dollar amount. Every care plan is individualized.

The program is available statewide, but applications go through the county MDHHS office where your parent lives. Timing and assessor availability can vary by county. The most important thing to know before you call: your parent must have active Michigan Medicaid (not just Medicare) to qualify.
programs.savingsSource: Free service; the program authorizes and pays for personal care services directly. No dollar amount or hour cap is published statewide by MDHHS.

summary: Must have active Michigan Medicaid (not Medicare alone)
Must need hands-on help with at least one daily task such as bathing or dressing
Must live at home or in an apartment, not a nursing facility
Must complete an in-home assessment by an MDHHS Adult Services Worker
A Medicaid-approved medical provider must certify the need in writing
structuredEligibility.functionalRequirement: Your parent must need hands-on physical assistance with at least one activity of daily living (ADL). ADLs include bathing, dressing, eating, grooming, moving around the home, transferring (getting in and out of a bed or chair), and toileting. Needing help only with housekeeping or errands, without a hands-on personal care need, is not enough to qualify. An MDHHS Adult Services Worker will conduct an in-home visit to assess this need and build a care plan.
otherRequirements: Must have active Michigan Medicaid Fee for Service coverage at the time of application and ongoing. Having Medicare alone does not qualify your parent.

A Medicaid-approved physician or other qualifying medical provider must complete form MDHHS-6200 (Adult Services Medical Needs Certification) confirming the need for care. A family member cannot fill out this form.
Your parent must live in a home or apartment in the community. People residing in nursing facilities are not eligible.
Your parent (or their legal guardian or representative) must sign the DHS-390 Adult Services Application.

applicationGuide.summary: Apply by contacting the county MDHHS office where your parent lives; no single statewide processing time is published, so start as early as possible.

steps.title: Confirm Medicaid is active
steps.description: Before anything else, verify your parent has active Michigan Medicaid Fee for Service coverage. If you are unsure, call the MDHHS Beneficiary Help Line at (800) 642-3195. Medicare alone is not enough to qualify.

steps.title: Contact your county MDHHS office
steps.description: Call, visit in person, mail, or fax a request to the county MDHHS office where your parent lives. Tell them you are requesting Home Help services. You can find your county office at michigan.gov/mdhhs or call the main MDHHS line at (855) 275-6424.

steps.title: Submit the DHS-390 application
steps.description: The county office will provide or accept a completed DHS-390 (Adult Services Application). This form must be signed by your parent or their legal guardian or authorized representative. Submit it to your county MDHHS office by mail, fax, or in person.

steps.title: Have your parent's doctor complete MDHHS-6200
steps.description: Ask your parent's Medicaid-approved physician or provider to complete the MDHHS-6200 (Adult Services Medical Needs Certification) form. This form must come from a qualifying medical provider; a family member cannot complete it. Return the completed form to the county MDHHS office.

steps.title: Complete the in-home assessment
steps.description: An MDHHS Adult Services Worker will schedule a home visit to assess your parent's needs. Be ready to describe specifically which daily tasks your parent cannot do without hands-on help. The assessor uses this visit to build your parent's individualized care plan and determine approved service hours.

steps.title: Services begin after authorization
steps.description: After the assessment is complete and the care plan is approved, the county office will authorize services and connect your parent with a provider. Service start timing depends on local MDHHS processing; no statewide guarantee is published.

applicationGuide.processingTime: No official statewide processing timeline is published by MDHHS. Timing depends on how quickly the referral, forms, and Adult Services Worker home visit can be completed at your county office. Starting early and submitting all documents at once reduces delays.
applicationGuide.waitlist: No formal statewide waitlist was identified in official MDHHS sources. Service start depends on local county processing capacity and how quickly the assessment and authorization are completed.
applicationGuide.tip: Submit the DHS-390 and the MDHHS-6200 at the same time, if possible. Applications stall most often when the medical certification form is missing or arrives late. Ask the county office for the MDHHS-6200 form at your first contact so you can get it to your parent's doctor right away.

applicationNotes: If your parent is being discharged from a hospital or skilled nursing facility, ask the discharge planner about starting a Home Help referral before they leave. Hospital social workers can sometimes initiate contact with MDHHS directly.

If your parent's condition worsens after they are enrolled, request a reassessment through the county MDHHS office. Approved hours can be adjusted if the Adult Services Worker determines the current plan no longer meets their needs.

Some third-party websites reference a form called the DHS-54A for medical certification. The official MDHHS program page names the MDHHS-6200 as the required form. Confirm with your county office which form they are currently using before asking your parent's doctor to complete it.

This program authorizes services, not cash. If a family member is providing the care and expects to be paid, that arrangement has specific rules under Michigan Medicaid. Ask the county MDHHS worker explicitly about whether a family caregiver can be enrolled as the paid provider under your parent's care plan.

contentSections.title: Medicare is not enough to qualify
contentSections.body: Your parent must have active Michigan Medicaid to be eligible for Home Help. Medicare, even with a supplement plan, does not qualify them. If your parent does not have Medicaid yet, contact MDHHS to ask about Medicaid enrollment before applying for Home Help.

contentSections.title: What the program covers
contentSections.body: Home Help can cover bathing, personal hygiene, dressing, grooming, mobility assistance inside the home, transferring (getting in and out of a bed or chair), toileting, help with eating, medication setup or administration, laundry, light housekeeping, meal preparation, and cleanup. The specific services authorized depend on what the MDHHS Adult Services Worker determines your parent needs during the in-home assessment.

faqs.question: My parent has Medicare and a supplement plan but not Medicaid. Do they qualify?
faqs.answer: No. Home Help requires active Michigan Medicaid, specifically Medicaid Fee for Service coverage. Medicare alone, including Medicare Advantage or a Medigap supplement, does not qualify your parent. If your parent might be eligible for Medicaid, contact MDHHS at (855) 275-6424 to ask about applying for Medicaid first.

faqs.question: Can I be paid to care for my own parent through this program?
faqs.answer: Possibly, but it depends on specific rules under Michigan Medicaid for family caregivers as paid providers. This is not automatic. When you speak with the county MDHHS Adult Services Worker during the assessment, ask directly whether a family member can be enrolled as the authorized paid provider under your parent's Home Help care plan.

faqs.question: My parent only needs help with housekeeping and grocery shopping. Does that qualify?
faqs.answer: Not on its own. To qualify, your parent must need hands-on physical assistance with at least one activity of daily living, such as bathing, dressing, getting out of bed, or toileting. Housekeeping alone, without a personal care need, does not meet the functional requirement. If your parent needs both, document the personal care needs clearly when you contact MDHHS.

faqs.question: How many hours of help will my parent actually get?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed statewide hour cap. The number of approved hours is determined individually by the MDHHS Adult Services Worker based on your parent's assessed needs. To get the most accurate outcome, be specific during the home visit about every daily task your parent cannot do safely on their own.

faqs.question: What if my parent's needs change after they are enrolled?
faqs.answer: Contact the county MDHHS office and request a reassessment. An Adult Services Worker can revisit the care plan and adjust authorized hours if your parent's condition has changed. There is no penalty for requesting a reassessment, and you do not have to wait for a scheduled review period.

faqs.question: How long will it take to get services started?
faqs.answer: No official statewide processing time is published by MDHHS. Timing depends on your county office's workload and how quickly the referral, both forms (DHS-390 and MDHHS-6200), and the in-home assessment can be completed. Submitting both forms at the same time and avoiding any documentation gaps is the most effective way to reduce delays.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply if they live in an apartment rather than a house?
faqs.answer: Yes. Home Help is available to people living in their own home or apartment in the community. The program is specifically for people in community settings, not nursing facilities or other institutional care.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my parent, or do they have to do it themselves?
faqs.answer: You can apply on behalf of your parent if you are their legal guardian, conservator, or authorized representative. You will need documentation of that legal authority, such as a guardianship order or a durable power of attorney for health care. The DHS-390 application must be signed by your parent or their authorized representative.

programs.name: Michigan Home Heating Credit
programs.tagline: If your parent rents or owns a home in Michigan and has a modest income, they may qualify for a state tax credit that offsets winter heating costs, with no age requirement and no asset test.
programs.intro:
If your parent lives in Michigan and pays for their own heat, either as a homeowner or a renter, they may qualify for the Michigan Home Heating Credit. This is a state tax credit that reduces the financial burden of heating costs. There is no age requirement, and there is no asset test. Eligibility is based on household size and annual income.

The credit is claimed by filing Form MI-1040CR-7 with the Michigan Department of Treasury. Your parent does not need to file a Michigan income tax return to claim it; the form can be submitted on its own. The income limits vary by household size: a single-person household qualifies with income up to $17,243 per year (2025 income, claimed in 2026), while a two-person household qualifies up to $23,185. The exact credit amount varies based on income, household size, and whether your parent rents or owns.

One critical deadline: the claim must be postmarked or received by September 30 each year. A tax extension does not extend this deadline. Filing early also results in priority processing. If your parent has never filed this claim before, or if it lapsed during a difficult year, this is worth revisiting now.
programs.savingsSource: The Michigan Department of Treasury does not publish a fixed statewide credit amount. The actual credit varies by household size, income level, and occupancy status. No specific dollar figures were available from official sources reviewed.

applicationGuide.summary: File Form MI-1040CR-7 online, by mail, or with your Michigan income tax return; the form is free and the deadline is September 30 each year.

steps.title: Get Form MI-1040CR-7
steps.description: Download the MI-1040CR-7 Home Heating Credit Claim and its Instruction Book from michigan.gov/taxes. You can also pick up a paper copy at a local library, MDHHS office, or community agency. The instruction book includes Table A, which shows the income ceiling for your parent's household size.

steps.title: Gather household information
steps.description: You will need: Social Security numbers and dates of birth for everyone in the household, total household income for the year, and rent or property tax information depending on whether your parent rents or owns. If your parent only lived in Michigan for part of the year, note the exact number of days occupied.

steps.title: Complete the form
steps.description: Use the instruction book to determine the correct number of household exemptions and locate the matching income ceiling in Table A. If household income is above the ceiling for that exemption count, the claim will not be approved. If income is within the limit, complete the remaining sections of MI-1040CR-7 based on whether your parent rents or owns.

steps.title: File by September 30
steps.description: If your parent also files a Michigan income tax return (MI-1040), attach MI-1040CR-7 to that return. If they do not file a Michigan income tax return, submit MI-1040CR-7 on its own. File online through Michigan Treasury e-filing options at michigan.gov/taxes, or mail the completed form to the Michigan Department of Treasury. The postmark or receipt date must be on or before September 30.

applicationGuide.processingTime: No official processing time is published. The Michigan Department of Treasury indicates that claims filed earlier receive priority processing.
applicationGuide.tip: Your parent can claim this credit even if they have never filed a Michigan income tax return. The form stands alone. If they missed prior years, each year's claim must be filed separately and by that year's deadline.

People in shared-housing situations (for example, multiple adults sharing a rental) do qualify, but the credit is prorated. Make sure to document the living arrangement accurately on the form.

If your parent moved into a licensed care facility or nursing home during the year, they may still qualify for a partial credit for the months they lived in their own homestead. The credit would be prorated based on days occupied.

contentSections.title: No Tax Return? Your parent can still file.
contentSections.body: Many older adults no longer file a Michigan income tax return because their income falls below the filing threshold. That does not disqualify them from the Home Heating Credit. Form MI-1040CR-7 can be filed on its own, completely separate from any income tax return.

faqs.question: My parent is in a nursing home now. Can they still claim this credit?
faqs.answer: Only if they did not live in the licensed care facility for the entire year. If your parent lived in their own home or rental for part of the year before moving, they may qualify for a prorated credit based on the days they occupied their homestead. They would not qualify if they were in a licensed care facility for all 12 months. Document the move-in date carefully when completing the form.

faqs.question: My parent shares a house with another adult. Does that disqualify them?
faqs.answer: No, but it reduces the credit. Shared-housing claims are prorated based on the living arrangement. Your parent still needs to file MI-1040CR-7 and document the shared-housing situation accurately. The instruction book for MI-1040CR-7 explains the proration calculation.

faqs.question: My parent has never filed a Michigan income tax return. Can they still get this credit?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Home Heating Credit does not require your parent to file a Michigan income tax return. Form MI-1040CR-7 can be submitted on its own to the Michigan Department of Treasury. Many lower-income seniors qualify for this credit precisely because their income is too low to trigger a state tax filing requirement.

faqs.question: We missed last year's September 30 deadline. Can we still file for that year?
faqs.answer: No. The September 30 deadline is strict and applies year by year. A missed deadline means that year's credit cannot be claimed. The best step now is to file for the current year before September 30. If you have questions about your specific situation, call the Michigan Department of Treasury at (517) 636-4486.

faqs.question: My parent got a tax extension. Does that push the heating credit deadline?
faqs.answer: No. A Michigan income tax filing extension does not extend the September 30 deadline for Form MI-1040CR-7. These are treated separately. Even if your parent's MI-1040 is on extension, the MI-1040CR-7 must still be postmarked or received by September 30.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly parent?
faqs.answer: Yes, with proper authorization. If you have power of attorney or are acting as your parent's legal representative, you can complete and file MI-1040CR-7 on their behalf. Include documentation of your authority with the filing. If you need help with the form, local libraries, MDHHS offices, and community agencies can assist. You can also call 2-1-1 to find local filing assistance.

faqs.question: My parent rents, but the landlord pays the utility bill directly. Can they still qualify?
faqs.answer: This depends on whether your parent is paying rent that covers heating costs. The eligibility rules distinguish between different occupancy and payment arrangements. Review the MI-1040CR-7 Instruction Book carefully, which walks through renter eligibility. If the situation is unclear, call the Michigan Department of Treasury at (517) 636-4486 before filing.

faqs.question: Is there an asset test? Would my parent's savings account disqualify them?
faqs.answer: No separate asset test was identified in the official program materials reviewed. Eligibility is based on household income and homestead status, not bank balances or property holdings. If this changes in a future program year, the Michigan Department of Treasury will publish updated instructions with Form MI-1040CR-7.

programs.intro:
If your aging parent is on a fixed income and struggling to keep up with energy bills in Michigan, the Michigan Energy Assistance Program (MEAP) can help pay electricity, natural gas, propane, heating oil, or other fuel costs for their primary home. MEAP also helps with past-due balances (arrearages) and can provide energy efficiency services depending on what the local provider offers.

MEAP is run through local community organizations across the state, not a single state office. That means the specific amount of help your parent receives, and how they apply, depends on which provider serves their county. The income limit for a one-person household is $36,043 per year (about $3,004 per month). If your parent already receives SSI, SNAP, TANF, or certain other public benefits, they may qualify automatically without needing to document their income separately.

The fastest way to find your parent's local MEAP provider is to call 2-1-1. That call connects you to the right local agency, which can then screen your parent for eligibility and walk you through the application. If your parent has a shutoff notice or is already past due, mention that immediately: some providers can move faster in crisis situations.
programs.savingsSource: MEAP benefit amounts are set by individual local providers within state program rules. No single statewide dollar figure is published. The Michigan Public Service Commission's official program page (michigan.gov/mpsc) describes the benefit as variable by provider and situation.

applicationGuide.summary: The simplest starting point is calling 2-1-1, which connects your parent to their local MEAP provider; processing time varies by provider and local demand.

steps.title: Call 2-1-1 to find your parent's local MEAP provider
steps.description: Dial 2-1-1 from any Michigan phone. Tell the operator you are looking for MEAP energy assistance. They will connect you to the local community agency that administers MEAP in your parent's county. Have your parent's address ready.

steps.title: Ask about intake options: phone, online, or in-person
steps.description: Local providers each run their own intake. Some, like Wayne Metro Community Action Agency, have an online application portal. Others take applications by phone or in-person appointment. Ask the local provider which method is fastest given current volume.

steps.title: Gather documents before the intake appointment
steps.description: Most providers will ask for proof of income, a recent utility bill, and proof of identity. If your parent receives SSI, SNAP, or another qualifying benefit, bring documentation of that enrollment instead of income records, because it may qualify them automatically.

steps.title: Submit the application through the local provider
steps.description: Complete the intake form the local provider gives you. There is no single statewide MEAP form. The provider reviews the application and determines the assistance package, which can include bill payment, arrearage help, or energy efficiency services.

steps.title: If there is a shutoff notice, say so immediately
steps.description: Tell the provider about any active disconnection notice or past-due balance at the start of the call. Some providers can expedite crisis cases. Do not wait until the end of the conversation to mention it.

applicationGuide.processingTime: No single statewide processing time is published. Timing depends on the local MEAP provider and current intake volume in your parent's area.
applicationGuide.waitlist: No statewide waitlist was identified in official MEAP materials. Availability depends on provider funding and local demand at the time of application.
applicationGuide.tip: If your parent already receives SSI, SNAP, or State Disability Assistance, mention that in the first sentence of the call. Categorical eligibility from those programs may allow the provider to skip income verification entirely, which speeds up the process.

contentSections.title: MEAP is not one program with one benefit amount
contentSections.body: Many families call expecting a fixed dollar credit, the way some other programs work. MEAP does not work that way. Your parent's local provider decides the actual assistance package: how much bill payment help, how much arrearage relief, and whether efficiency services are included. Two families in different Michigan counties with identical incomes and bills may receive different amounts. That is by design. The amount is set by the local provider within state program rules, not by a state schedule.

contentSections.title: Already on SSI, SNAP, or SDA? You may not need income documents.
contentSections.body: If your parent already receives SSI, SNAP/FAP, TANF/FIP, WIC, Head Start, State Emergency Relief, Home Heating Credit, or State Disability Assistance, they may qualify for MEAP categorically. That means their enrollment in one of those programs may substitute for income verification. Mention this at the start of your call to the local provider.

faqs.question: My parent's utility is threatening to disconnect service. Can MEAP stop that in time?
faqs.answer: Possibly, but you need to act immediately. Call 2-1-1 today and tell the operator your parent has an active disconnection notice. Some local MEAP providers have crisis pathways that move faster than standard processing. Also ask whether Michigan's State Emergency Relief (SER) program through MDHHS can help in parallel, since SER is specifically designed for urgent situations. Do not wait for the disconnection to happen before calling.

faqs.question: Can I apply for MEAP on behalf of my elderly parent, or do they have to call themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can apply as an authorized representative or on your parent's behalf. Have your parent's basic information ready: their address, utility account details, income sources, and the names and birthdates of everyone in the household. Let the provider know at the start of the call that you are the adult child helping your parent apply.

faqs.question: My parent's income is just above the limit for a single person. Is there any flexibility?
faqs.answer: The income ceiling for a one-person household is $36,043 per year (about $3,004/month) under the 60% State Median Income rule. If your parent lives with you or other household members, the limit is higher because it adjusts by household size: $47,279 for two people, $58,515 for three. If household size is being counted incorrectly, that could affect eligibility. Ask the provider how they are defining your parent's household before assuming they do not qualify.

faqs.question: My parent already gets SSI. Do they still need to go through the full application?
faqs.answer: SSI is one of the categorical qualifying programs for MEAP, which means SSI enrollment may substitute for income documentation. Your parent still needs to contact their local MEAP provider and complete intake, but the process may be simpler. Bring the SSI award letter to the appointment or have it ready for the call.

faqs.question: Can my parent get help with both electricity and natural gas through MEAP?
faqs.answer: MEAP covers electricity, natural gas, propane, heating oil, and other deliverable fuels used for heat. Whether your parent gets help with one or multiple fuel types depends on what the local provider offers and what your parent's situation requires. Ask the provider specifically what types of energy costs they can address.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply for MEAP and the Michigan Home Heating Credit at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and they are different programs. The Home Heating Credit is a Michigan state tax credit claimed on the MI-1040CR-7 form when filing state taxes. MEAP is a direct assistance program administered through local community agencies. Qualifying for one does not prevent your parent from using the other. Ask the MEAP provider whether they can also screen your parent for SER or other overlapping programs at the same time.

faqs.question: What if my parent rents and the landlord pays the utility bills?
faqs.answer: MEAP assistance is for a primary residence, and eligibility is tied to the household that uses the energy. If your parent's utility costs are included in their rent and the account is in the landlord's name, eligibility for MEAP in that situation is something to raise directly with the local provider. Bring any lease documentation that shows what your parent pays for and to whom. The provider will tell you whether the arrangement qualifies.

faqs.question: How do I know which local provider serves my parent's county?
faqs.answer: Call 2-1-1 from any Michigan phone. The operator will identify the correct local MEAP provider for your parent's address and connect you. You can also visit michigan.gov/mpsc and look under energy assistance resources. Wayne County residents can contact Wayne Metro Community Action Agency directly at (313) 388-9799.

stateOverview.intro: Michigan offers 5 key programs that can help your aging loved one stay independent and reduce your family's caregiving costs. These range from comprehensive home care services (Michigan Choice Waiver) to free grocery assistance navigation (MiCAFE) to volunteer companionship. Most programs focus on seniors with limited income, but some resources like Senior Companion Program are available regardless of finances. Start by checking if your loved one qualifies for the Michigan Choice Waiver Program or MI Health Link, these provide the most comprehensive support and can save thousands in care costs. For immediate help, MiCAFE offers free assistance getting your loved one enrolled in SNAP benefits within days.
